objectives: Name a major key by counting the sharps or flats in its signature
A major has three sharps; B♭ major has two flats and E♭ major three
Sharps and flats each arrive in a fixed order, so the count alone names the key

concept.title: Counting the signature
concept.body: Grade 1 gave you two sharp keys and one flat key. Three more follow the same rule. A major has three sharps: F♯, C♯ and G♯. B♭ major has two flats, B♭ and E♭; E♭ major has three, adding A♭. The sharps always arrive in the order F♯ C♯ G♯ and the flats as B♭ E♭ A♭, never in a different order and never skipping one, so the count alone names the key. Read the signature left to right, count what you see, and stop. Notice that the second flat, E♭, is also the name of the key that has three of them.

teach.smartTip: Count them: three sharps is A major; two flats is B♭ major, three flats is E♭ major.
teach.didYouKnow: Flats are written in the order B, E, A, D, G, C, F — exactly the sharp order (F, C, G, D, A, E, B) reversed.

objectives: The three relative pairs: A minor with C major, E minor with G major, D minor with F major
A key and its relative minor or major always share the same key signature
How to count a minor 3rd down from a major tonic to find its relative minor

concept.title: Grade 2 relative minor keys
concept.body: Every major key has a relative minor that shares its key signature. C major and A minor both have no sharps or flats; G major and E minor both have one sharp, F♯; F major and D minor both have one flat, B♭. The relative minor's tonic sits a minor 3rd below its major partner's.

teach.smartTip: Count three semitones — a minor 3rd — down from the major tonic and you'll land on the relative minor, two letter-names lower: C down to A, G down to E, F down to D.
teach.didYouKnow: A relative major and minor share every note in their scale, yet sound completely different — because their home note, the tonic, is different.

objectives: Harmonic minor is the natural minor with the 7th note raised
Where the scale's semitones fall — three of them, plus the augmented 2nd between the 6th and 7th notes
The raised 7ths for A, E and D minor: G♯, D♯ and C♯

concept.title: Grade 2 harmonic minor
concept.body: Harmonic minor is built from the natural (key-signature) minor scale with one change: the 7th note is raised a semitone. That raised 7th creates an augmented 2nd — a gap of three semitones — between the 6th and 7th notes, which is what gives harmonic minor its distinctive sound. A minor's raised 7th is G♯, E minor's is D♯, and D minor's is C♯.

teach.smartTip: The 7th is raised with an accidental, written note by note — it is never written in the key signature.
teach.didYouKnow: The augmented-2nd gap between the 6th and 7th notes is what gives harmonic minor its distinctive, almost exotic sound.

objectives: Name any note of a major scale by its degree number
The keynote is the 1st degree, so the count starts at one, not zero
The rule is the same in A, B♭ and E♭

concept.title: Counting from the keynote
concept.body: The rule you learned at Grade 1 does not change with the key. The keynote is the 1st degree and the numbers count up the letter names from it. What changes is which notes those numbers land on. In B♭ major the 1st degree is B♭, the 2nd is C, the 3rd is D. In A major the 1st is A and the 3rd is C♯. Read the key signature first, decide the keynote, then count. Minor keys number the same way from their own keynote.

teach.smartTip: Read the key signature, find the keynote, then count letter names up from it.
teach.didYouKnow: This is why a singer can be told 'you are flat on the 3rd' without anyone naming a note. The degree number is the same instruction in every key.

lessons.title: Tonic triads in the new keys

objectives: Build the tonic triad of a major key in root position
The tonic triad is the 1st, 3rd and 5th degrees stacked
Root position means the keynote is the lowest note

concept.title: Three notes that fix the key
concept.body: The tonic triad is still the 1st, 3rd and 5th degrees stacked, whatever the key. In B♭ major that gives B♭, D and F; in E♭ major, E♭, G and B♭. The key signature supplies any flat or sharp, so you rarely need to write an accidental — build the triad from the letter names and let the signature do the rest. A minor key's tonic triad works the same way from its own keynote.

teach.smartTip: Keynote, skip, skip. The key signature supplies the accidentals; you supply the letters.
teach.didYouKnow: Because the pattern is always 1-3-5, a player can find the tonic triad of an unfamiliar key without knowing a single one of its notes by name.
